meta.sources: U.S. EIA (energy prices) and FRED/BLS (producer price indexes)
meta.row: one price series in one month
meta.rebasing: Every series is indexed to 100 at January 2019. The levels sit in different units ($/mcf, ¢/kWh, index points) and are never drawn on a shared value axis. Indexing is what makes one axis honest.
meta.caution: An index shows relative movement from the base month only. A series that starts high and stays flat looks identical to one that is cheap and flat.
meta.stages: feedstock → resin → product. The chain has three links, and ‘did output prices follow input prices down’ is unanswerable with only the last one. Retracement is the share of a series’ rise above its base month that has since come back.
meta.base_month_bias: January 2019 is a winter month, so gas enters the index at a seasonal high and its later fall looks larger than an annual-average base would show. The stage ordering below is robust to that; the exact percentages are not.
meta.not_margin: An output index rising faster than an input index is not a margin. Labour, freight, energy and packaging are not in either series. It is a spread between two published indices, and that is all it is.
meta.definition: Retracement is (peak − now) ÷ (peak − 100): the share of a series’ rise above its January 2019 base that has since come back. A series that never rose above that base has no retracement and is not drawn on the ladder.
meta.scope: No economy-wide comparator is drawn against the converter spread. The shipped series carry no total-manufacturing input and output pair, so whether every downstream industry held price this way over these years is a question this page cannot answer.
